points.t: Small pustules, each pierced by a hair, on the beard, scalp, thighs, buttocks or axillae, often after shaving, waxing or occlusion.
Inflammation of the follicle opening, usually S. aureus. Pseudomonas (hot tubs), Malassezia, or irritant/occlusive causes are possible.
Stop the trigger, use an antiseptic wash, and topical or oral flucloxacillin only if persistent or extensive.
Progression to boils or cellulitis, recurrent disease (carriage, diabetes) and immunosuppression.

Topical steroids and immunosuppression increase risk.
**Follicular-centred pustules**, often with a hair visible in the centre, on a red base.
Sites: scalp, beard (sycosis barbae), trunk, buttocks, thighs and axillae.
Itchy or tender. Systemic upset is unusual.

cards.name: Acne vulgaris
cards.clue: Comedones present; face, chest and back; mixed lesion types

cards.name: Pustular miliaria
cards.clue: Heat and occlusion; tiny pustules not centred on follicles

cards.name: Candida
cards.clue: Satellite pustules around a red, moist fold

cards.name: Keratosis pilaris
cards.clue: Rough follicular papules on the upper arms and thighs; not pustular

items.t: Progression to **boils, carbuncles or cellulitis**, or fever.
Recurrent disease despite measures: consider carriage, PVL or MRSA, diabetes and immunosuppression.
Widespread itchy folliculitis in an immunosuppressed patient (eosinophilic): refer.

pearls.t: **Pustules on the upper back and chest after antibiotics?** Think Pityrosporum folliculitis, which needs an antifungal.
A hot-tub history explains a sudden ‘swimsuit-distribution’ rash.
Most mild bacterial folliculitis settles without antibiotics, which is a useful stewardship opportunity.
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is common in curly hair. Discuss shaving technique and beard growth sensitively.
